title: Atopic Dermatitis: Repair the Barrier, Control the Inflammation
bottomLine: Atopic dermatitis is chronic relapsing inflammatory skin disease. Daily emollient barrier care plus appropriately potent topical anti-inflammatory therapy is more effective than avoiding every possible trigger or using antibiotics for noninfected flares.
recognize: Pruritic eczematous patches vary by age and skin tone; flexural disease is common in older children/adults.
differentiate: Scabies causes intense nocturnal itch and household spread; contact dermatitis follows exposure pattern; impetiginization adds crusting/oozing.
assessment: Assess itch/sleep, distribution, infection, bathing/products, occupational exposure, food allergy history and psychosocial burden.
workup: Routine allergy panels are not indicated without a convincing immediate food-allergy history.
management: Use fragrance-free moisturization and site-appropriate topical corticosteroids or steroid-sparing agents; treat secondary infection only when clinically present.
medicationSafety: Avoid high-potency topical steroids on face and skin folds for prolonged courses; fear of all topical steroids can cause undertreatment.
counselling: Explain proactive maintenance for recurrent sites and that skin of colour may show grey, brown or violaceous inflammation rather than bright erythema.
followUp: Escalate refractory moderate/severe disease for phototherapy or systemic/biologic options.
examTrap: Ordering broad food allergy testing for every child with eczema and no immediate food reactions.
oneLinePearl: Eczema treatment is barrier repair plus inflammation control—not trigger hunting alone.

title: Psoriasis: Skin Disease With Joint and Cardiometabolic Consequences
bottomLine: Psoriasis is chronic immune-mediated disease; assess extent, special sites, quality of life, psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic comorbidity. Treatment intensity should reflect total disease burden, not body-surface area alone.
recognize: Well-demarcated plaques, scalp disease and nail pitting are common; inverse psoriasis affects folds and may lack scale.
differentiate: Tinea, eczema and seborrheic dermatitis can mimic localized disease; new hot painful joints require septic/crystal differential.
assessment: Assess nails, scalp/genitals, joints/entheses, obesity, diabetes, smoking, mood and treatment preference.
workup: Diagnosis is usually clinical; biopsy is reserved for atypical cases. Baseline infection/lab testing depends on systemic treatment.
management: Use topical therapy for limited disease and phototherapy/systemic or biologic therapy for more severe or high-impact disease.
medicationSafety: Systemic immunomodulators require infection, pregnancy and organ-specific monitoring.
counselling: Explain links with psoriatic arthritis and cardiovascular risk.
followUp: Track both skin and joint symptoms.
examTrap: Calling severe genital or palmoplantar psoriasis 'mild' because total body surface area is small.
oneLinePearl: Psoriasis severity is impact plus location plus extent, not percentage alone.

title: Acne and Rosacea: Similar Face, Different Inflammation
bottomLine: Comedones point toward acne; persistent centrofacial erythema, flushing and inflammatory papules without comedones suggest rosacea. Treat early enough to reduce scarring and psychosocial harm.
recognize: Acne can include comedonal, inflammatory and nodulocystic lesions; rosacea can include ocular symptoms.
differentiate: Perioral dermatitis, steroid acne and lupus rash can mimic facial inflammatory disease.
assessment: Assess severity/scarring, pregnancy, medications/cosmetics, mental-health impact and ocular symptoms.
workup: Routine laboratory testing is unnecessary for typical acne or rosacea; isotretinoin requires pregnancy-prevention and therapy-specific monitoring.
management: Use topical retinoid/benzoyl peroxide and selected antimicrobial or hormonal therapy for acne; use trigger/skin-care measures and topical or systemic rosacea therapy by phenotype.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged antibiotic monotherapy for acne and avoid potent topical steroid combinations on the face; isotretinoin is highly teratogenic.
counselling: Set expectations that acne treatment requires weeks and gentle skin care.
followUp: Escalate scarring, refractory or severe disease.
examTrap: Prescribing topical clindamycin alone for months without benzoyl peroxide or an antimicrobial-resistance strategy.
oneLinePearl: Comedones separate acne from many acne-like facial eruptions.

title: Urticaria and Angioedema: Is the Airway Involved?
bottomLine: Hives alone are usually histamine-mediated skin disease; angioedema with airway, breathing or circulatory compromise is anaphylaxis until treated. Recurrent angioedema without hives can be bradykinin-mediated and will not respond reliably to antihistamines.
recognize: Urticaria lesions are transient raised pruritic wheals that typically migrate and resolve within 24 hours at one site.
differentiate: Urticarial vasculitis lesions last longer, hurt or bruise; ACE-inhibitor angioedema commonly lacks hives.
assessment: Assess airway/voice, breathing, BP, GI symptoms, medication and food/sting exposure, lesion duration and ACE inhibitor use.
workup: Routine allergy panels are not indicated for chronic spontaneous urticaria without a specific trigger history.
management: Use non-sedating H1 antihistamines for urticaria; use IM epinephrine immediately for anaphylaxis; stop ACE inhibitor in ACE-associated angioedema.
medicationSafety: Antihistamines do not replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis; first-generation antihistamines can impair driving and increase falls.
counselling: Teach epinephrine auto-injector use and emergency plan when anaphylaxis risk exists.
followUp: Refer recurrent unexplained anaphylaxis or angioedema for allergy/immunology evaluation.
examTrap: Giving diphenhydramine first while delaying epinephrine for hypotension and wheeze.
oneLinePearl: Skin symptoms can wait; anaphylaxis cannot.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology resources

title: Cellulitis or Abscess: Antibiotics Do Not Drain Pus
bottomLine: Nonpurulent cellulitis is diffuse bacterial skin infection; a fluctuant abscess requires incision and drainage for source control. Bilateral red lower legs are rarely bilateral cellulitis and should prompt pseudocellulitis alternatives.
recognize: Cellulitis causes unilateral warmth, tenderness and spreading erythema; abscess produces a focal tender collection.
differentiate: Venous stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, gout and DVT can mimic cellulitis.
assessment: Assess systemic illness, immune status, diabetes, wound/portal, fluctuance, pain out of proportion and exposure risks.
workup: Routine blood cultures and imaging are unnecessary in uncomplicated mild cellulitis; ultrasound helps when occult abscess is uncertain.
management: Drain abscesses; use narrow antibiotics for cellulitis based on severity and local epidemiology; urgently escalate necrotizing infection concern.
medicationSafety: Do not add unnecessary MRSA coverage to every nonpurulent cellulitis without risk/context.
counselling: Elevate affected limb and mark progression when useful; explain expected early response.
followUp: Reassess non-improvement for abscess, resistance, pseudocellulitis or deeper infection.
examTrap: Treating bilateral chronically edematous red legs as bilateral cellulitis.
oneLinePearl: Bilateral lower-leg redness should make cellulitis less likely, not more.

title: Herpes Zoster: Treat Early, Protect the Eye
bottomLine: Painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution suggest herpes zoster. Antiviral therapy is most useful early and is especially important with ophthalmic, neurologic, disseminated or immunocompromised disease.
recognize: Neuropathic pain can precede the rash; lesions usually respect a dermatome and midline.
differentiate: HSV can recur in localized clusters; contact dermatitis is pruritic rather than neuropathically painful.
assessment: Assess eye/forehead/nose involvement, cranial nerves, immune status, pregnancy contacts and dissemination.
workup: Typical disease is clinical; PCR is useful for atypical lesions.
management: Use antiviral therapy and pain control; urgent ophthalmology for V1/ocular symptoms and hospital-level treatment for disseminated/severe immunocompromised disease.
medicationSafety: Renal adjustment is needed for acyclovir/valacyclovir; avoid topical antivirals as sole therapy for zoster.
counselling: Cover lesions and avoid exposing susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts until lesions crust; discuss zoster vaccination after recovery when eligible.
followUp: Manage postherpetic neuralgia if pain persists.
examTrap: Treating ophthalmic zoster as a routine skin rash without eye assessment.
oneLinePearl: Zoster on the forehead is an eye question until proven otherwise.

title: Tinea and Scabies: Morphology, Microscopy, Contacts
bottomLine: Annular scaly lesions suggest dermatophyte infection; intense nocturnal itch with household spread and burrows suggests scabies. Treat the organism and exposure pattern—do not suppress either with potent steroid combinations that distort the rash.
recognize: Tinea often has active scaly edge and central clearing; scabies favours finger webs, wrists, waist/genitals and can be atypical in infants/older adults.
differentiate: Eczema, psoriasis and granuloma annulare can mimic tinea; crusted scabies in immunocompromised/older adults is highly contagious.
assessment: Assess contact spread, pets, travel/communal living, steroid use and immune status.
workup: KOH scraping or fungal culture can clarify atypical tinea; scabies is often clinical but dermoscopy/scraping can confirm.
management: Use site-appropriate topical/systemic antifungal; treat scabies patient and close contacts simultaneously and manage linens/environment according to guidance.
medicationSafety: Avoid potent steroid-antifungal combination creams, especially on face/folds, because they can cause atrophy and tinea incognito.
counselling: Scabies itch can persist after mites are eradicated; persistent itch alone does not prove treatment failure.
followUp: Reassess morphology if antifungal/scabies treatment fails.
examTrap: Escalating steroid potency for a spreading annular fungal rash.
oneLinePearl: Steroids can hide fungus while the fungus keeps growing.

title: Skin Cancer: Change, Nonhealing, and the Ugly Duckling
bottomLine: A changing pigmented lesion, ugly-duckling mole, nonhealing ulcer or keratinizing lesion deserves diagnostic assessment and often biopsy. Melanoma risk is driven by evolution and morphology, not simply lesion size.
recognize: ABCDE features support melanoma suspicion; BCC often pearly/ulcerated; SCC may be scaly, keratotic or nonhealing.
differentiate: Seborrheic keratoses and benign nevi can look irregular but stability and dermoscopic/clinical pattern matter.
assessment: Assess evolution, sun/tanning exposure, immune suppression, prior skin cancer and family melanoma history; examine regional nodes when suspicious.
workup: Biopsy technique should preserve accurate histopathologic staging when melanoma is possible; avoid destructive treatment before diagnosis.
management: Refer or excise according to lesion and local pathway; suspected melanoma requires prompt definitive biopsy and staging care.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly treat an undiagnosed nonhealing lesion with topical steroids or antibiotics.
counselling: Recommend sun protection and avoidance of artificial tanning; teach self-skin checks.
followUp: Risk-based surveillance after skin cancer diagnosis.
examTrap: Shaving or destroying a suspicious pigmented lesion without ensuring adequate pathology for melanoma diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: A changing lesion needs tissue, not another cream.
sourceBasis: Canadian Dermatology Association skin cancer resources and 2026 tanning statement

title: SJS/TEN: Mucosal Erosion Plus Skin Pain Is an Emergency
bottomLine: Skin pain, rapidly evolving dusky lesions or blisters and mucosal erosions after a medication can signal Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Stop the culprit drug immediately and transfer for specialized supportive care.
recognize: Fever and prodrome may precede painful skin and oral, ocular or genital mucosal disease.
differentiate: Simple drug exanthem is usually not painful and lacks mucosal detachment; DRESS has different timing and systemic features.
assessment: Assess airway, eye/genital involvement, skin detachment, hemodynamics and all recent new medications.
workup: Diagnosis is clinical supported by dermatology and often biopsy; assess organ/electrolyte complications.
management: Stop suspected culprit drugs, use burn/ICU-level supportive care when extensive and obtain dermatology/ophthalmology input.
medicationSafety: Never rechallenge a likely culprit medication after SJS/TEN.
counselling: Document the culprit drug prominently and provide future avoidance information.
followUp: Long-term ocular, mucosal and psychological sequelae may require specialty care.
examTrap: Continuing a newly started high-risk medication while treating the rash with antihistamines because it is called an allergy.
oneLinePearl: Painful skin plus mucosa after a new drug is not a routine drug rash.
sourceBasis: Canadian dermatology and critical-care practice principles

title: Sinusitis: Viral Until Duration or Pattern Says Bacterial
bottomLine: Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral. Bacterial disease becomes more likely with persistent symptoms without improvement, severe early illness or double-worsening after initial improvement; imaging is not routine in uncomplicated cases.
recognize: Purulent nasal discharge alone does not prove bacterial infection.
differentiate: Allergic rhinitis is recurrent/itchy and afebrile; orbital cellulitis causes eye swelling/pain and is emergent.
assessment: Assess duration, double-worsening, fever, unilateral facial pain, orbital/neurologic symptoms and immune status.
workup: No routine sinus x-ray/CT for uncomplicated acute disease; image suspected orbital/intracranial complication or atypical severe disease.
management: Use analgesia and intranasal saline/steroid where appropriate; use narrow antibiotic treatment when bacterial criteria are met.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical decongestant use because rebound rhinitis can occur.
counselling: Explain why green mucus can occur in viral infection.
followUp: Reassess treatment failure for complication or alternate diagnosis.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because nasal discharge turned green on day four of a cold.
oneLinePearl: Bacterial sinusitis is a time-course diagnosis, not a mucus-colour diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Sore Throat: Test for GAS When the Clinical Probability Fits
bottomLine: Most pharyngitis is viral. Use age-appropriate clinical probability to decide whether to test for group A streptococcus; treat confirmed bacterial infection rather than prescribing empirically for every exudative throat.
recognize: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and oral ulcers favour viral disease; tender anterior nodes, fever and tonsillar exudate support GAS.
differentiate: Peritonsillar abscess causes muffled voice/trismus and unilateral swelling; epiglottitis causes drooling/toxic airway symptoms; EBV can cause posterior adenopathy.
assessment: Assess airway, hydration, cough/coryza, rash, neck swelling, trismus, sexual exposure and immune status.
workup: Use rapid antigen or throat culture according to age and local pathway; avoid routine testing when viral features dominate.
management: Provide analgesia/hydration and treat confirmed GAS with narrow therapy; drain/ENT assess abscess.
medicationSafety: Amoxicillin can produce a rash in EBV and should not be interpreted automatically as IgE allergy.
counselling: Explain that antibiotics do not shorten ordinary viral sore throat meaningfully.
followUp: Reassess worsening unilateral or airway symptoms.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics for tonsillar exudate without testing in a stable patient whose diagnosis is uncertain.
oneLinePearl: Exudate is not a synonym for strep.
sourceBasis: Canadian antimicrobial stewardship and ENT practice resources

title: Otitis Externa: Treat the Canal, Protect High-Risk Patients
bottomLine: Pain with tragal or pinna movement and an inflamed ear canal suggests otitis externa. Topical therapy is usually preferred; severe pain, cranial neuropathy or diabetes/immunocompromise raises malignant otitis externa concern.
recognize: Swimming, canal trauma and hearing devices can predispose.
differentiate: AOM is middle-ear disease; mastoiditis affects postauricular area; Ramsay Hunt has vesicles/facial palsy.
assessment: Assess canal swelling/discharge, tympanic membrane visibility/integrity, diabetes/immune status and cranial nerves.
workup: Culture is reserved for recurrent/refractory or high-risk disease; imaging for malignant otitis externa concern.
management: Use topical antibiotic with or without steroid according to tympanic membrane status and wick when canal is markedly swollen; urgent ENT for invasive disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid ototoxic drops when tympanic membrane perforation cannot be excluded unless the product is safe for middle-ear exposure.
counselling: Keep canal dry and avoid cotton swab trauma.
followUp: Reassess lack of improvement within 48–72 hours.
examTrap: Prescribing oral antibiotics alone for uncomplicated diffuse otitis externa.
oneLinePearl: Otitis externa is a topical canal infection until high-risk features say otherwise.

title: Epistaxis: Pressure First, Source Second
bottomLine: Most anterior nosebleeds stop with correct sustained compression. Heavy posterior bleeding, airway compromise, hemodynamic instability or anticoagulant-associated major bleeding requires escalation and source control.
recognize: Dryness, trauma/nose picking and anticoagulants are common contributors.
differentiate: Hemoptysis and hematemesis can be confused with swallowed posterior nasal blood.
assessment: Assess airway, hemodynamics, duration, anticoagulants, bleeding disorder, trauma and visible source.
workup: CBC/coagulation testing is reserved for significant/recurrent bleeding or relevant comorbidity; routine labs are unnecessary for minor isolated epistaxis.
management: Sit forward and compress the soft cartilaginous nose continuously; use topical vasoconstrictor/cautery or packing when needed and ENT for posterior/refractory bleeding.
medicationSafety: Do not stop anticoagulation permanently for minor nosebleeds without considering the thrombotic indication.
counselling: Teach exactly where and how long to pinch the nose and avoid tilting the head back.
followUp: Recurrent unexplained unilateral bleeding may need ENT evaluation.
examTrap: Pinching the bony bridge of the nose for two minutes and calling compression unsuccessful.
oneLinePearl: Correct epistaxis pressure is low, soft, firm, and sustained.

title: Red Eye: Pain, Vision Loss, and Photophobia Are the Triage Questions
bottomLine: Simple conjunctivitis should not cause severe pain, marked photophobia or major visual loss. Those features suggest keratitis, uveitis, acute angle closure, scleritis or other sight-threatening disease and require urgent eye assessment.
recognize: Conjunctivitis often causes diffuse redness and discharge with preserved vision; bacterial versus viral distinction is imperfect.
differentiate: Corneal abrasion/keratitis causes pain and photophobia; uveitis causes ciliary flush; angle closure adds severe pain, headache, nausea and high intraocular pressure.
assessment: Check visual acuity in each eye, pupils, pain/photophobia, contact lens use, trauma/chemical exposure and corneal appearance.
workup: Use fluorescein examination when corneal injury is possible; tonometry is used when glaucoma is suspected and is not contraindicated by possible globe rupture.
management: Treat cause; chemical exposure requires immediate irrigation before history is complete; contact-lens keratitis needs urgent ophthalmology and antipseudomonal coverage.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe topical anesthetic for unsupervised home use and avoid steroid eye drops without ophthalmic diagnosis.
counselling: Stop contact lens use during painful/red eye until safely assessed.
examTrap: Calling a painful photophobic contact-lens red eye conjunctivitis and giving routine antibiotic drops without corneal assessment.
oneLinePearl: Red eye plus pain or vision loss is not routine conjunctivitis.

title: Sudden Vision Threat: Angle Closure, Retinal Detachment, Vascular Occlusion
bottomLine: Sudden painful vision loss suggests angle closure or inflammatory/corneal disease; sudden painless monocular loss suggests retinal or vascular emergency. Do not defer abrupt vision loss to routine optometry follow-up.
recognize: Retinal detachment may cause flashes, new floaters and a curtain; central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden profound painless loss; angle closure causes severe eye pain, headache, halos and nausea.
differentiate: Migraine aura is usually bilateral visual-field phenomenon and transient; vitreous floaters alone may be benign but new flashes/field loss are not.
assessment: Check visual acuity, pupils including RAPD, fields, eye pain/redness, neurologic symptoms and vascular risk.
workup: Use tonometry/slit lamp/fundus assessment where trained and immediately involve ophthalmology; suspected retinal artery occlusion also triggers stroke/vascular evaluation.
management: Treat angle closure immediately with pressure-lowering protocol and ophthalmology; urgent retinal repair pathway for detachment; vascular occlusion requires emergency specialty evaluation.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergic/sympathomimetic drugs can precipitate angle closure in susceptible anatomy.
counselling: New flashes, floaters plus field loss require same-day emergency assessment.
followUp: After acute treatment, manage vascular and fellow-eye risk.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with new floaters and a curtain because there is no eye pain.
oneLinePearl: Painless does not mean harmless when vision disappears suddenly.
sourceBasis: Canadian Ophthalmological Society clinical practice principles
